source: Workbook of Attached - Amir Levine, Rachel Heller

assets.domain: Attachment Theory | Biological Need for Connection
assets.topic: The Biological Imperative of Human Attachment
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen showing a mother holding her newborn while fMRI brain scans glow orange in the attachment centers, contrasted with a solitary figure in a sparse room whose stress-hormone levels spike visually as red cortisol waves pulse around their silhouette.
assets.player_mission: Audit 12 social scenarios and identify which ones meet the biological criteria for genuine attachment connection vs. mere social interaction. Highlight moments where the hypothalamus activates or blood pressure changes signal true attachment distress.
key_concepts: Attachment is a deep, long-lasting bond creating desire to stay in touch
Emotional connection provides a solid foundation that reduces stress
Hypothalamus less active when holding partner hand under stress
Unhappy relationships cause elevated blood pressure and health risks

assets.topic: Recognizing Your Need for Safe Haven
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple sitting in a therapist office with a conversational UI overlay showing "attachment bids" in real-time: one partner reaches for the other and a glowing "CONNECTION SOUGHT" tag appears, with response options labeled "Soothing," "Dismissive," or "Neutral."
assets.player_mission: Play as a partner who feels distressed after a long day. Navigate 6 conversational turns where you must articulate your need for connection without triggering conflict. Score points each time you express vulnerability clearly and lose points when you mask distress with criticism.
key_concepts: Everyone needs connection for healthy and happy life
Distress arises when we sense our partner will not be available
Solid emotional foundation buffers against life stressors
Physical health is linked to relationship quality

assets.topic: The "I Dont Need Anyone" Myth
assets.visual_frame_description: A psychological profile dossier with redacted case notes, showing a subject who claims complete independence but whose biometric data reveals elevated cortisol, poor sleep, and increased illness rates. Margin notes read: "Subject denies attachment needs — biology disagrees."
assets.player_mission: Review 8 personal testimonies from individuals who claim they do not need close relationships. Cross-reference their claims against physiological data, life outcomes, and long-term health records. Identify which subjects are deceiving themselves and flag the rationalization patterns they use.
key_concepts: Attachment need is built into DNA, not learned behavior
Evolutionary roots trace back to survival through mutual dependence
Genetic propensity to attach is universal across humans
Denying attachment needs leads to measurable health deterioration

assets.topic: Distinguishing True Attachment from Casual Connection
assets.visual_frame_description: A 3x4 grid of scenarios: a coffee chat with a coworker, a deep talk with a partner after a crisis, a transactional exchange with a cashier, a child clinging to a parent after a nightmare, etc. Each cell has a slider for "Attachment Depth" from 0 to 10.
assets.player_mission: Classify 12 social scenarios along the attachment spectrum. Drag each scenario onto a matrix with axes "Emotional Significance" and "Distress at Separation." Correct placement reveals whether the bond meets the scientific criteria for attachment.
key_concepts: Attachment involves deep emotional bond and desire to stay in touch
Not all social bonds qualify as attachments
Signs of genuine attachment include distress at separation and comfort from presence
Secure attachments buffer stress; insecure ones amplify it

assets.topic: The Partnership Stress Test: Secure Base or Stress Source?
assets.visual_frame_description: A final boss arena shaped like a giant human heart with arteries as pathways. The boss "Cortisol King" hurls red stress waves. Your shield is a glowing orb labeled "Secure Connection." Partner NPCs stand by offering different types of support.
assets.player_mission: Face 4 waves of stressors (work crisis, health scare, social rejection, existential dread). In each wave, choose the right type of support from a partner to minimize your stress response. Wrong choices (dismissiveness, criticism, withdrawal) multiply incoming damage. Defeat the boss by demonstrating that genuine attachment connection is the ultimate stress buffer.
key_concepts: Hypothalamus activity decreases with partner support under stress
Secure connection provides a calming physiological effect
Attachment is not optional but a biological requirement
Relationship quality directly impacts long-term health outcomes

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Our Desire for Connection Is Inherited and Shaped by Upbringing

assets.topic: Parental Influence on Attachment Wiring
assets.visual_frame_description: A split timeline showing two children: one whose parents respond sensitively to cries (warm orange glow around attachment brain regions) and one whose parents are neglectful (cold blue, underdeveloped neural pathways). Time-lapse aging shows how early patterns become adult relationship templates.
assets.player_mission: Review 10 parent-child interaction transcripts spanning infancy through adolescence. Identify each interaction as "Secure-Building," "Anxiety-Inducing," or "Avoidance-Reinforcing." Flag moments where parental attunement or misattunement shapes long-term attachment architecture.
key_concepts: Parents shape attachment through caregiving style and responsiveness
Secure parent-child bonds predict healthy adult relationships
Tumultuous adult relationships can also reshape attachment patterns
Attachment style is influenced by both genes and life experiences

assets.topic: Breaking the Generational Attachment Pattern
assets.visual_frame_description: A living room where a parent and adult child sit together. A conversational UI shows "Legacy Patterns" floating like ghosts behind each speaker. The parent says something dismissive, and the player can choose to respond from their own feelings or from the old pattern.
assets.player_mission: Play as an adult who recognizes their attachment patterns stem from childhood. Navigate 8 conversations with your parents about emotionally charged topics. Each time you respond differently than your childhood programming dictates, you weaken the old neural pathway and strengthen a new secure pattern.
key_concepts: Childhood experiences shape genetic propensity to attachment
Secure parenting — attention and appropriate responsiveness — builds secure adults
Tumultuous romantic engagements later can negatively reshape attitudes
Attachment patterns are malleable throughout life

assets.topic: The "I Turned Out Fine" Rationalization
assets.visual_frame_description: A case file on a subject who insists their cold upbringing was "character building." Biometric data, relationship history, and therapy notes contradict the claim. Red underlines highlight discrepancies between stated beliefs and actual behavior patterns in relationships.
assets.player_mission: Examine 7 personal narratives where individuals claim their upbringing had no negative effect on their relationships. Cross-reference with attachment interviews, partner reports, and physiological stress responses. Identify whose self-assessment is accurate vs. who is using intellectualization as a defense mechanism.
key_concepts: Parents who form secure bonds produce children with secure patterns
Knowing difference between child wanting affection vs. hunger is key
Childrens failure to form bonds is not always parents fault
Adult relationships can heal or further damage attachment patterns

assets.topic: Separating Genetic Propensity from Learned Behavior
assets.visual_frame_description: A twin-study matrix showing identical twins raised apart, fraternal twins raised together, adopted siblings, and biological siblings. Each cell maps their attachment styles onto a scatter plot with "Genetics Score" and "Upbringing Score" axes.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 15 case pairs and determine for each whether the attachment outcome is better explained by genetics, upbringing, or their interaction. Place each pair on a matrix and receive accuracy feedback based on attachment research findings.
key_concepts: Attachment urge is built into human DNA
Life experiences can affect genetic propensity
Parents attitudes about relationships shape childs worldview
Relationships later in life can also affect attachments

assets.topic: The Ancestral Attachment Gauntlet
assets.visual_frame_description: A multi-generational family tree comes alive as a boss arena. Each ancestor is a mini-boss embodying their attachment style: the dismissive great-grandfather throws avoidance shields, the anxious grandmother casts worry chains. You fight through generations to reach the final boss: "Inherited Pattern."
assets.player_mission: Progress through 4 generations of attachment patterns. In each generation, identify the dominant style and choose interventions that prevent transmission to the next generation. Successfully break 3 of 4 negative cycles to defeat the final boss and unlock the "Conscious Reparenting" achievement.
key_concepts: Parents responsiveness to child signals shapes attachment
Secure relationships later can repair insecure early patterns
Both genetic and environmental factors contribute to attachment style
Understanding ones origins helps in making conscious relationship choices

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Anxious Attachment — Need for Closeness and Reassurance

assets.topic: Spotting Anxious Activation Triggers
assets.visual_frame_description: A nervous system dashboard showing real-time readings for an anxiously attached person. When their partner does not respond to a text immediately, alarms flash: heart rate spikes, cortisol surges, catastrophizing thoughts appear as scrolling text. The cue scrubber highlights each trigger point.
assets.player_mission: Monitor 15 interaction logs between an anxiously attached individual and their partner. Identify which specific partner behaviors trigger anxious activation (delayed response, ambiguous language, withdrawal). Flag false alarms where the trigger was misinterpreted and the partner had a benign explanation.
key_concepts: Anxious preoccupied individuals obsess about partner love and commitment
Small partner behaviors get magnified and personalized
Constant contact is desired and its absence causes distress
Emotional stability from a partner is crucial for anxious individuals

assets.topic: Expressing Needs Without Accusation
assets.visual_frame_description: A phone screen showing a text conversation. The anxiously attached user types a message full of worry: "You didnt respond for 3 hours. Are you mad at me?" The simulation offers alternative phrasings that express the same need without triggering avoidant defenses.
assets.player_mission: Play as an anxiously attached individual whose partner has been distant for a day. Navigate 8 conversational turns where you must express your need for reassurance while avoiding protest behaviors (criticism, clinging, testing). Each successful calm communication earns attachment security points.
key_concepts: Anxious type requires closeness and is preoccupied with relationships
People with anxious style constantly worry partner does not love them enough
Seeing missed call as rejection is classic anxious pattern
Need someone with emotional resources to provide stability

assets.topic: The "Im Just Being Realistic" Self-Deception
assets.visual_frame_description: A therapy intake form where the patient describes themselves as "realistic about relationships." Margin annotations from a therapist note: "Patient describes catastrophic interpretations of partner behavior as realism — reframe needed." Attachment style quiz results reveal anxious preoccupied pattern.
assets.player_mission: Review 6 self-assessments from individuals who describe themselves as appropriately cautious in relationships. Compare their self-descriptions against their actual behavior logs and partner feedback. Identify cases where anxious attachment is masked as realism or intuition.
key_concepts: Anxious individuals personalize partner actions excessively
They fear partner does not love them enough
Catastrophic interpretations of ambiguous partner behavior are common
Self-awareness of attachment style is first step to secure functioning

assets.topic: Anxious vs. Secure vs. Avoidant Responses to Distance
assets.visual_frame_description: A 3x4 grid showing three people (Anxious, Secure, Avoidant) responding to the same scenario: partner is working late and unreachable. Anxious person sends 12 texts, Secure person leaves one message and waits, Avoidant person feels relieved. Each cell shows thought bubbles.
assets.player_mission: Classify 18 responses to relationship scenarios as Typical Anxious, Typical Secure, or Typical Avoidant. Scenarios include: partner forgets a date, partner is quiet at dinner, partner wants solo vacation. Correct classification reveals the attachment logic behind each response.
key_concepts: Anxious style marked by desire for constant contact
Tendency to take partner actions personally
Look for someone willing and capable of meeting need for availability
Secure partner can make anxious person feel truly loved and understood

assets.topic: The Worry Monster: Calming the Anxious Mind
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena inside an anxious mind. The Worry Monster fires thought-missiles: "Theyre pulling away," "Im not enough," "Theyre going to leave." Your shield is labeled "Self-Soothing" and your special attack is "Reality Check" — calibrated against actual evidence.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the Worry Monster across 4 phases, each corresponding to a different anxiety trigger (unreturned text, cancelled plans, distracted partner, ambiguous future talk). In each phase, distinguish real relationship threats from anxiety-generated false alarms. Only counter-attack when the threat is real.
key_concepts: Anxious attachment type is preoccupied with relationship security
Partners unavailability triggers intense distress and worry
Finding a partner with emotional resources is essential
Secure partner provides constant reassurance and availability

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Avoidant Attachment — The Pursuit of Independence

assets.topic: Detecting Avoidant Deactivation Cues
assets.visual_frame_description: A relationship dashboard tracking an avoidant individuals proximity tolerance. When a partner gets "too close" emotionally, red zones flash: distancing behaviors activate (focus on partner flaws, prioritizing work, creating space). A needle labeled "Intimacy Tolerance" swings toward "Danger."
assets.player_mission: Analyze 12 relationship scenarios where an avoidant individual begins deactivating. Identify the specific distancing strategies used: flaw-finding, independence-asserting, space-creating. Determine which strategies are unconscious defenses vs. conscious choices.
key_concepts: Avoidant individuals preserve autonomy and fear losing independence
They avoid becoming too close for fear of losing freedom
Hard time recognizing others emotions, making connection difficult
Have a set image of ideal relationship and struggle with compromise

assets.topic: Bridging the Distance Without Smothering
assets.visual_frame_description: A living room where one partner sits on one couch, the other far away. A conversational interface shows "Intimacy Thermometer" rising and falling. When the avoidant partner feels pressured, a visual barrier of ice forms between them.
assets.player_mission: Play as the partner of an avoidant individual. You want more closeness but must navigate 10 conversational turns without triggering their deactivation system. Choose requests that express your needs while respecting their autonomy. Each successful bid for connection that does not trigger withdrawal earns intimacy points.
key_concepts: Avoidants irritated by small partner flaws as excuse for distance
They struggle to make concessions based on partner needs
Quick to blame others when relationship has difficulties
Need to view partner in positive light rather than as problem source

assets.topic: The "I Just Need Space" Rationalization Pattern
assets.visual_frame_description: A series of relationship termination reports. Each shows an avoidant individuals explanation for breakup: "They werent my type," "Too clingy," "Not the one." A pattern analysis overlay reveals the underlying commonality: all relationships ended when intimacy reached a certain threshold.
assets.player_mission: Review 8 relationship histories from self-identified "independent" individuals who have had multiple short-term relationships. Identify the pattern of deactivation-and-exit that repeats when intimacy deepens. Flag rationalizations that mask fear of closeness.
key_concepts: Avoidants maintain emotional distance by searching for "the one"
Small partner imperfections become excuses to keep searching
They must think about partner in favorable way to make relationships work
Conflict resolution requires looking for cause of conflict inside self

assets.topic: Healthy Autonomy vs. Avoidant Withdrawal
assets.visual_frame_description: A matrix with axes "Time Apart" and "Emotional Connection When Together." Four quadrants: Healthy Autonomy (high connection, reasonable space), Avoidant Withdrawal (low connection, much space), Anxious Clinginess (high need, little space), Disorganized (erratic). Each quadrant has illustrative couples.
assets.player_mission: Classify 14 couple behavior patterns into the correct quadrant. For each pattern, assess whether the distance serves healthy autonomy or defensive avoidance. Scenarios include a partner taking a solo trip, working late repeatedly, having separate friend groups, or refusing to discuss feelings.
key_concepts: Avoidant attachment style seeks independence in relationship
They feel trapped when partner is too reliant
Hard time recognizing others emotions
Need to search for conflict cause inside themselves

assets.topic: The Independence Fortress: Lowering the Drawbridge
assets.visual_frame_description: A castle fortress surrounded by a moat labeled "My Independence." The drawbridge only lowers when approached with exactly the right pressure — too much force and it stays locked, too little and nothing happens. Partner NPCs approach with varying degrees of closeness.
assets.player_mission: Play as an avoidant individual who wants to let someone in. Navigate 5 levels of intimacy, each requiring you to lower defenses. At each level, choose responses that allow connection without triggering your flight response. Success means keeping the drawbridge open without feeling engulfed.
key_concepts: Avoidants can prevent strain by being ready to put in effort
Must think of partner in good light rather than as problem cause
Search for conflict cause inside self, viewing through partner eyes
Independence does not have to mean isolation

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Secure Attachment — The Go-With-the-Flow Advantage

assets.topic: Recognizing Secure Base Behaviors
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple interacting fluidly throughout a day. When one partner is stressed, the other offers support without being asked. When one needs space, the other grants it without resentment. Each interaction gets a green "Secure" tag with the specific behavior highlighted.
assets.player_mission: Observe 20 couple interactions and identify which behaviors characterize secure attachment: comfort with intimacy, appropriate responsiveness, non-defensive communication, accurate reading of partner needs. Flag imitations where a behavior looks secure but is actually anxious compliance or avoidant distancing in disguise.
key_concepts: Secure individuals are at ease with proximity and intimacy
They can read between the lines and understand partner needs without excessive concern
Greatest predictor of good relationship is being with a secure partner
Even one secure partner can enhance relationship quality

assets.topic: Embodying the Secure Partner Response
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple in conflict — one partner snaps harshly due to stress. A "Secure Response" option glows: partner does not take it personally, sees the stress behind the words, and offers support. The visual shows how this de-escalates the situation compared to anxious or avoidant alternatives.
assets.player_mission: Play as the partner of someone who is stressed and irritable. Navigate 8 exchanges where your partner snaps, withdraws, or criticizes. In each, practice the secure response: do not personalize, see the need behind the complaint, offer support without fixing. Score points for maintaining connection through the storm.
key_concepts: Secure individuals unconcerned with excessive or insufficient reliance
They know how to read between the lines
Best predictor of good relationship is having secure partner
One secure partner can alleviate issues caused by different attachment type

assets.topic: The "We Dont Fight" Illusion
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple profile labeled "Perfect Relationship — No Conflict." Deeper investigation reveals they avoid all difficult conversations. True secure profiles show moderate conflict with healthy repair. The audit flags the difference between genuine security and conflict-phobic pseudo-harmony.
assets.player_mission: Review 10 relationship profiles claiming to be "secure." Dig beneath the surface to distinguish genuine secure attachment (comfortable with intimacy, handles conflict well) from pseudo-security (avoidance masquerading as harmony, or anxious clinging mislabeled as closeness).
key_concepts: Secure individuals comfortable with intimacy and independence
They read partner needs without being overly concerned or disinterested
They handle partners harsh remarks by recognizing stress behind them
They find ways to help and encourage without being asked

assets.topic: Secure vs. Anxious vs. Avoidant Conflict Resolution
assets.visual_frame_description: A 3x3 grid showing the same conflict scenario resolved by Anxious, Avoidant, and Secure individuals. Anxious sends 20 texts analyzing it, Avoidant pretends it did not happen, Secure addresses it calmly. Each cell shows the short-term relief vs. long-term outcome.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 15 conflict scenarios and predict how each attachment style would handle them. Then classify the actual resolution strategies shown. Learn the differential outcomes: secure resolution builds trust, anxious resolution creates temporary relief but reinforces worry, avoidant resolution leaves issues festering.
key_concepts: Secure partners are comfortable with both closeness and independence
They provide emotional stability without being overbearing
They can handle partner criticism without becoming defensive or dismissive
Relationships between two secure individuals have fewest difficulties

assets.topic: The Storm of Insecurity: Holding Steady as a Secure Base
assets.visual_frame_description: A ship in a storm. Your partner is drowning in anxiety. As the secure base, you must throw lifelines (validation, presence, reassurance) while anchors labeled "Fix It" and "Minimize" threaten to drag you down. The storm has 4 waves of increasing intensity.
assets.player_mission: Serve as the secure partner for someone with anxious attachment going through a crisis. Through 4 escalating waves of partner distress, resist the temptation to either over-function (rescuing) or under-function (withdrawing). Maintain your own emotional regulation while providing steady support. Each wave passed strengthens the relationships attachment bond.
key_concepts: Secure individuals maintain composure under relationship stress
They do not take partners bad moods personally
They can provide comfort while maintaining own emotional balance
Even one secure partner transforms the relationship dynamic

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Finding and Keeping Love Through Communication

assets.topic: Identifying Communication Patterns That Build or Break Connection
assets.visual_frame_description: A communication dashboard showing transcripts of couples conversations. Effective communications are highlighted in green (specific, non-blaming, need-stating) and ineffective in red (vague, accusatory, avoidant). A running score shows relationship health impact of each exchange.
assets.player_mission: Audit 25 communication snippets from dating scenarios. Classify each as Effective (states need without blame), Ineffective-Vague (hints without clarity), or Ineffective-Accusatory (blames without owning feelings). Calculate the ratio needed for relationship success.
key_concepts: Good communication is the key regardless of attachment type
Stating wants and concerns openly makes partner compatibility assessment easier
Understanding signals from someone you just started dating is difficult
Bring up difficult subjects directly instead of worrying silently

assets.topic: The "Hasnt Made a Move" Conversation
assets.visual_frame_description: Two people on a date. A thought bubble shows one worrying: "Why hasnt he kissed me? Does he not like me?" The simulation offers a direct approach option where the player can ask about intentions without sounding needy.
assets.player_mission: You have been on 5 dates with someone who has not initiated physical intimacy. Navigate a conversation where you bring this up directly without accusations. Choose phrasings that express your feelings and ask about their perspective. Success means both people feel heard.
key_concepts: Good communication helps locate and retain ideal spouse
Stating wants and worries openly reveals partner compatibility
Bring up subject directly instead of worrying
Asking directly is a great and effective method to learn their perspective

assets.topic: The "They Should Just Know" Fallacy
assets.visual_frame_description: Case files on individuals who ended promising relationships because their partner "should have known" what they needed. Each case shows the unspoken expectations, the eventual disappointment, and the pattern of assuming mind-reading should occur in love.
assets.player_mission: Examine 8 relationship post-mortems where the stated reason for breakup was "they should have known what I needed." Identify the specific uncommunicated expectations in each case. Calculate how many of these breakups could have been prevented by one direct conversation.
key_concepts: Effective communication means bringing up issues without blaming partner
Express concerns without assigning blame for better understanding
Everyone expectations must be on the table for relationship to work
Precision about issue is the key to successful communication

assets.topic: Blaming vs. Owning: Two Ways to Raise an Issue
assets.visual_frame_description: A 2x3 grid showing the same complaint phrased different ways. Left column: blaming versions ("You never listen"). Right column: owning versions ("I feel unheard when..."). Each cell shows the defensive reaction vs. the connecting reaction from a partner.
assets.player_mission: Transform 12 blaming statements into owning statements. Place each on a matrix of "Specificity" vs. "Blame Level." Learn the formula: "I feel [emotion] when [specific behavior] happens. I need [specific need.]" Practice until the blaming-to-owning conversion is automatic.
key_concepts: Expressing wants directly prevents concerns from building up
Be precise about issue without blaming partner
"Talking about your ex makes me sad and insecure" is effective
Non-blaming expression ensures the other person understands your view

assets.topic: The Compatibility Conversation: Navigating Make-or-Break Topics
assets.visual_frame_description: A gauntlet of 5 conversation rooms, each containing a high-stakes relationship topic: marriage, children, finances, values, and life goals. A compatibility meter rises or falls based on how each conversation is handled.
assets.player_mission: Progress through 5 critical relationship conversations. In each, choose between avoiding the topic, attacking the partner, or communicating openly. Open communication increases compatibility score and reveals true alignment. Avoidance or blame decreases it and wastes time in incompatible relationships.
key_concepts: Not every single issue needs to be brought up immediately
Key is preventing concerns from building up
Precision about issue without blaming is essential
Expressing concerns without blame helps others understand your perspective

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Making Relationships Work Through Conflict Coping

assets.topic: Identifying Healthy vs. Destructive Conflict Patterns
assets.visual_frame_description: A conflict analysis dashboard showing a couples argument mapped in real-time. Productive patterns glow green (staying on topic, concern for partner, seeking compromise) and destructive patterns glow red (kitchen-sinking, personal attacks, stonewalling).
assets.player_mission: Review 15 conflict transcripts and identify escalation markers. Flag when couples generalize ("You always..."), kitchen-sink (bring up unrelated grievances), or attack character vs. behavior. Determine which conflicts are productive (leading to understanding) vs. destructive (leading to resentment).
key_concepts: Conflict is an unavoidable element of every relationship
It is not how much you disagree but how you disagree that matters
Avoid broad generalizations during disagreements
Limiting debate to a single subject prevents escalation

assets.topic: The Grocery Store Fight: Keeping Conflict Productive
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple in a kitchen arguing about groceries. The argument starts specific but threatens to expand. The interface shows branching paths: stay on topic vs. expand the fight. Red flags appear when generalizations are used.
assets.player_mission: Navigate a disagreement about household responsibilities. Through 7 conversational turns, resist the urge to bring up past grievances or make sweeping generalizations. Stay on one topic. Each time you limit the scope, the argument resolves more quickly and constructively.
key_concepts: Disagreement about groceries should not spill into dishes argument
Limiting scope of debate to single subject prevents escalation
Be concerned about partners well-being during conflict
Finding good compromises on difficult topics satisfies everyone

assets.topic: The "We Never Fight" Red Flag
assets.visual_frame_description: A relationship audit dossier for a couple who claims they never argue. Investigation reveals unspoken resentments building silently over years. The file contrasts this with a secure-couple file showing regular, constructive disagreements that deepen intimacy.
assets.player_mission: Examine 6 relationship histories where couples pride themselves on never fighting. Dig into the hidden costs: unspoken needs, growing distance, sudden breakups that surprise everyone. Compare against couples who fight productively and report higher satisfaction.
key_concepts: Arguing with spouse can make you happier when done right
Finding good compromises on difficult topics is essential
Disagreements can be opportunity to strengthen attachment connection
Bringing up long-troubling issues allows partner to see your side

assets.topic: Compromise vs. Accommodation vs. Capitulation
assets.visual_frame_description: A 3x3 grid showing the same conflict resolved three ways: true compromise (both give a little, both get a little), accommodation (one gives in), capitulation (one gives up resentfully). Each cell shows the short-term relief and long-term relationship health outcome.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 12 conflict scenarios and classify the resolution approach used. Determine whether each resolution is a genuine compromise that strengthens the bond, an accommodation that creates imbalance, or a capitulation that builds resentment.
key_concepts: Conflict is unavoidable element of every relationship
Whats important is how you disagree, not how much
Finding compromises ensures everyone is satisfied with situation
Resolving conflict helps everyone in the end

assets.topic: The Conflict Spiral: Breaking the Escalation Cycle
assets.visual_frame_description: A spiral staircase descending into darkness, representing an escalating argument. At each level, the boss "Escalation Demon" offers you worse responses: sarcasm, contempt, stonewalling. You must choose repair attempts at each level to reverse direction and climb back up.
assets.player_mission: Face 4 levels of conflict escalation. At each level, the argument has intensified. Choose a repair attempt — humor, admission of fault, expressing appreciation, or requesting a pause — to de-escalate. Each successful repair attempt reduces the spiral level. Reaching the top means the conflict became an intimacy-building opportunity.
key_concepts: Conflict can strengthen attachment when handled constructively
Partners cannot read minds — issues must be voiced
Talking about anger leads to relief for both partners
Ending the guessing game about wants and desires benefits the relationship

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Dont Settle — Knowing When a Partner Cant Meet Your Needs

assets.topic: Spotting the Anxious-Avoidant Trap
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple on a roller coaster labeled "Anxious-Avoidant Relationship." The track alternates between thrilling highs (intense reunion after conflict) and terrifying lows (silent treatments, withdrawal). A warning dashboard flags the pattern and predicts the crash.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 10 relationship histories between anxious and avoidant partners. Identify the predictable cycle: anxious pursues, avoidant withdraws, anxious escalates, avoidant distances further, anxious apologizes, temporary harmony, repeat. Flag exit points where the cycle could have been broken.
key_concepts: Movie myth: real love can bring any relationship together regardless of differing needs
Anxious and avoidant types create a roller coaster relationship
Opposing views on intimacy strain major life decisions like marriage and children
Finding companion who can fulfill your needs is key to successful relationship

assets.topic: The Incompatibility Conversation: When to Walk Away
assets.visual_frame_description: A couple having a painful but honest conversation about fundamental incompatibility. The interface shows both partners needs profiles and highlights where they clash irreconcilably: one wants marriage and children, the other wants freedom and autonomy.
assets.player_mission: You are in a relationship with someone who cannot meet your core attachment needs. Navigate 6 conversations where you must honestly assess compatibility. At the end, decide whether to stay (accepting unmet needs) or leave (seeking better match). The simulation scores you on honesty with yourself and partner.
key_concepts: Real love does not have power to bring any relationship together
Essential need for lasting relationship is sharing true love
Not everyone has the same requirements from relationships
If cant agree on important life choices, compromise is nearly impossible

assets.topic: The "Love Conquers All" Self-Deception
assets.visual_frame_description: A case file on a couple who insisted love would overcome their fundamental incompatibility. Evidence includes: therapy bills, police call records, tearful journal entries. The audit concludes: they ignored attachment style mismatch for years before the inevitable collapse.
assets.player_mission: Review 7 case studies of couples who stayed together despite fundamental attachment incompatibility. Identify each couples rationalization pattern ("Well grow together," "We balance each other out," "Hes great except for..."). Calculate the cost in years lost before finally accepting the mismatch.
key_concepts: Anxious and avoidant attachment types are particularly problematic together
Opposing intimacy views affect marriage and children decisions
Anxious individuals often desire marriage and children, avoidants do not
Finding someone who can meet needs is ultimate key to success

assets.topic: Mapping Your Attachment Needs Against a Partners Capacity
assets.visual_frame_description: A compatibility matrix with axes "My Need for Closeness" and "Partners Capacity for Closeness." Five zones: Thriving (both high), Balanced (both moderate), Mismatched-Anxious (high vs. low), Mismatched-Avoidant (low vs. high), Toxic (low vs. low). Each zone shows relationship trajectory.
assets.player_mission: Complete a self-assessment of your own attachment needs, then evaluate 12 potential partners profiles. Place each on the compatibility matrix and determine the predicted relationship trajectory. Learn which mismatches can be bridged and which are fundamental deal-breakers.
key_concepts: Most essential need for long-lasting relationship is shared true love
But genuine compatibility requires matching needs for intimacy
Knowing what spouse needs and letting them know what you need is vital
If not really pleased, do not spend time on unsolvable problems

assets.topic: Walking Away from the Wrong Relationship
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a heart with cracks running through it. The final boss is "Sunk Cost" — a massive figure made of all the time, energy, and memories invested in a relationship that cannot meet your needs. Your weapon is "Self-Respect."
assets.player_mission: You are in a relationship with fundamentally mismatched attachment needs. The boss attacks with emotional manipulation tactics: guilt ("After all weve been through"), fear ("Youll never find anyone else"), hope ("I can change"). Defeat Sunk Cost by recognizing these as traps. The final blow is choosing yourself.
key_concepts: Accepting incompatible desires and needs is sometimes best course
Looking for someone with expectations more aligned with yours is the solution
This is how you keep your relationship pleasant
Knowing your own attachment type helps find a compatible partner

chapters.title: Final Conclusion: Applying Your Attachment Knowledge

assets.topic: Synthesizing Your Attachment Style Profile
assets.visual_frame_description: A comprehensive dashboard showing your attachment style assessment results across multiple dimensions: need for closeness, sensitivity to rejection, comfort with independence, conflict style, and communication patterns. Each dimension has a score and growth recommendations.
assets.player_mission: Review a synthesized attachment profile based on all previous chapter learnings. Identify your dominant pattern, your secondary tendencies, and your blind spots. Receive personalized recommendations for partner selection and communication improvement.
key_concepts: Dont leave anything to chance in long-term relationship
First determine your personal attachment type
Then look for mate who can provide what you desire and need
Knowing attachment type helps understand and express requirements

assets.topic: Your Attachment Action Plan: Implementing Changes
assets.visual_frame_description: A planning session where you design your relationship strategy going forward. The interface shows your attachment profile, your typical triggers, and a set of communication tools. You build a personalized action plan.
assets.player_mission: Create and test your personal attachment action plan. Role-play 6 scenarios where your old patterns would have kicked in. Practice new responses based on what you have learned. Each successfully navigated scenario reinforces the new neural pathway.
key_concepts: Tell spouse if you have an issue with them
Letting little issue linger is bad for relationship
Express dissatisfaction without allowing other problems to distract
Make effort to determine your unique attachment style

assets.topic: The Relationship Pattern Audit: Honest Inventory
assets.visual_frame_description: A final audit dossier compiling all your past relationship patterns. The file contrasts what you thought was happening in past relationships with what attachment science reveals was actually happening. Margin notes highlight recurring themes.
assets.player_mission: Complete a final honest audit of your relationship history. Review 5 past relationships through the lens of attachment theory. Identify what attachment style each partner likely had, what style you brought, and where the mismatch occurred. The goal is clarity without self-blame.
key_concepts: Get deeper knowledge of yourself and your needs for happy relationship
Knowing attachment type helps find partner who can meet them
Dont leave anything to chance in long-term relationships
Clear communication is the foundation of healthy partnership

assets.topic: The Complete Partner Compatibility Matrix
assets.visual_frame_description: A comprehensive 5x5 matrix combining all dimensions of attachment compatibility: style match, communication quality, conflict resolution approach, needs alignment, and life goals harmony. Each potential partner can be plotted and scored.
assets.player_mission: Apply the full attachment framework to evaluate 10 potential partners (or past partners). Score each across all 5 dimensions of compatibility. Learn which dimensions are deal-breakers vs. negotiable and how to identify a genuinely compatible partner.
key_concepts: Knowing attachment type helps better understand and express requirements
Locating partner who can meet your needs requires self-knowledge
Every relationship requires active communication and effort
Compatibility is not magic — it is measurable and learnable

assets.topic: The Relationship Mastery Final Exam: All Lessons Combined
assets.visual_frame_description: A final boss arena combining elements from all previous battles. The first wave tests attachment style identification, the second wave tests communication in conflict, the third wave tests compatibility assessment, and the final wave tests the ability to walk away from a bad match.
assets.player_mission: A comprehensive final exam with 4 waves covering all 8 chapters of the workbook. Wave 1: Identify attachment styles from behavior descriptions. Wave 2: Choose effective communication in difficult conversations. Wave 3: Assess compatibility between different style combinations. Wave 4: Make the right decision in a high-stakes relationship choice. Pass all waves to earn the "Attachment Master" achievement.
key_concepts: Integration of all attachment principles
Self-knowledge is the foundation of relationship success
Theory without action is incomplete — apply what you learn
Relationships can be understood scientifically and improved consciously
